extracted.intended_audience: registered patent attorneys and agents; USPTO disciplinary counsel; attorneys facing reciprocal discipline
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures the USPTO applies when considering imposing reciprocal discipline based on a state's disciplinary adjudication (37 C.F.R. §11.24), including the defenses a practitioner must prove to avoid identical discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process (Selling element (i))
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner may avoid imposition of identical reciprocal discipline by clearly and convincingly demonstrating that the procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute a deprivation of due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(i) quoted: 'The procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute a deprivation of due process.' The Office examines whether the practitioner had a reasonable opportunity and whether any asserted lack of motivation to litigate elsewhere negates the due process contention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infirmity of proof (Selling element (ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner may avoid reciprocal discipline by clearly and convincingly demonstrating there was such an infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept the other jurisdiction's conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(ii) quoted. The practitioner must produce clear and convincing evidence (not mere assertions) that the record from the other jurisdiction is so infirm that USPTO cannot accept its findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice (Selling element (iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal discipline may be avoided if the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates that imposition of the same discipline by the USPTO would result in grave injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iii) quoted. The Office will evaluate claims (e.g., delay, mitigation, mistaken factual findings) but requires clear and convincing proof that accepting the other jurisdiction's sanction would be gravely unjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other argument that practitioner was not suspended (Selling element (iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may present any argument that the practitioner was not properly suspended/disbarred in the other jurisdiction as a defense to reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iv) (text identifies other permissible arguments). The Office will consider whether the asserted lack of valid suspension/disbarment undermines the reciprocal discipline request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final adjudication establishes prima facie case (37 C.F.R. §11.24(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: A final adjudication in another jurisdiction that a practitioner has been guilty of misconduct establishes a prima facie case by clear and convincing evidence that the practitioner violated 37 C.F.R. 10.23 (as further identified under 37 C.F.R. 10.23(c)(5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(e) quoted. This creates a presumption in favor of imposing reciprocal discipline unless one of the Selling exceptions is clearly and convincingly demonstrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO rule 10.23 substantive standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not engage in disreputable or gross misconduct and shall not engage in any conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a),(b) quoted. Rule 10.23(c) lists examples; paragraph (c)(5) specifically includes 'suspension or disbarment from practice as an attorney or agent on ethical grounds by any duly constituted authority of a State' as conduct constituting a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: State suspension/disbarment as independent ground
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspension or disbarment from a state bar on ethical grounds constitutes, on its face, a violation of USPTO ethics rules without requiring that the specific state rule be identical to an Office rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office treats state disciplinary suspension as a ground for USPTO sanction per 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(5); USPTO will not require a precise match between the state rule and USPTO rule to impose reciprocal discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof (respondent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The respondent/practitioner has the burden to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that one of the Selling elements precludes reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts have generally held it is the respondent's burden to show (by clear and convincing evidence) that a Selling element applies; this is an uphill burden and the norm is to impose substantially similar discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norm of imposing substantially similar discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The norm in reciprocal-discipline cases is for the federal authority (USPTO) to impose discipline substantially similar to that imposed by the state court or authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities (e.g., In re Lange, In re Barach) establish that unless a Selling exception is proven, the Office will impose the same or substantially similar sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business transaction vs fee agreement (RPC 1.8(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A fee agreement does not amount to a 'business transaction' requiring special protections unless it includes a promise of something other than cash payment; complex fee terms may transform a fee agreement into a business transaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ABA Model Rule 1.8 Comment 1 referenced: 'a fee agreement does not amount to a business transaction unless it includes a promise of something other than cash payment.' The Office evaluates terms such as advancing of cash, payment of another practitioner's bills, discounted rates for risk, and interest provisions to determine whether the agreement went beyond a simple fee arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy underlying RPC 1.8(e) (loans/funding settlements)
rubrics_metrics.description: RPC 1.8(e) (and DR 5-103(B)) is designed to protect clients from the danger that an attorney's financial involvement (e.g., loans to fund settlement) will impair independent judgment and induce settlement for financial reasons rather than merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedent (e.g., Shea v. Virginia State Bar) recognizes the policy; the Office will consider the risk that attorney-funded settlements undermine client independence and generally expects practitioners to abide by the restriction or seek rule change rather than disregard it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of attorney-client relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an attorney-client relationship exists depends largely on the client's subjective belief reasonably formed based on the attending circumstances, including the attorney's words or actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court language quoted (Bohn v. Cody): the Office will consider the client's declaration and the facts/circumstances (agreement terms, attorney's representations) to determine whether the client reasonably believed the attorney continued to represent them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of mitigating and aggravating factors in discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanction determinations take into account mitigating factors (e.g., delay between conduct and charges) and aggravating factors (e.g., misconduct benefitted attorney at client's expense, continued denial of wrongdoing, extensive experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state court's balancing of mitigation and aggravation is noted by the Office; such factors inform whether a one-year suspension was appropriate, but do not necessarily prevent USPTO from imposing identical discipline absent a Selling exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural obligations when suspended and reinstatement eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A suspended practitioner must comply with duties under 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 while suspended and may apply for reinstatement under 37 C.F.R. § 11.60 after the period specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order directs publication of notice in the Official Gazette, notice to USPTO employees and interested agencies/courts, and specifies the effective date and reinstatement eligibility (one year from effective date in this case).
